questions.question:
The following sentence has been split into four segments. Identify the segment that contains a grammatical error:

As he is not satisfied / with the jury's decision, / he appeal / in the higher court.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is **Option 1**.

 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The verb form "**appeal**" is incorrect here because the sentence is in the present tense referring to a single subject "he."
 
• The correct verb form should be "**appeals**" to maintain subject-verb agreement.
 
• "He appeals in the higher court" is grammatically accurate and conveys the intended meaning.
 
• Thus, the error lies in **segment 1: 'he appeal'**.

Therefore, the correct answer is **Option 1**.

 

**Correct Sentence:** *"As he is not satisfied with the jury's decision, he **appeals** in the higher court."*

 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Option 2: "with the jury's decision"** – This is grammatically correct and appropriately structured.
 
• **Option 3: "in the higher court"** – Although "to the higher court" is more common, "in" is not grammatically incorrect.
 
• **Option 4: "As he is not satisfied"** – This is a properly framed conditional phrase.

questions.question:

questions.solution:

• **"Honorary"** refers to a title or position given as an honor without requiring the performance of usual duties. (मानद)

• Hence, the correct spelling is **"Honorary"**.

Therefore, the correct answer is: **Honorary**.

• **Example:** He received an honourary title for his contributions to the arts.
 
 
 
• **Hononary** (मानद): Incorrect spelling; not a valid word in English.

questions.question: Select the option that has an error in the usage of the present perfect tense.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is **Option 3**.

 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• In the sentence "**Reh has complete his homework**", the verb "**complete**" is incorrectly used.
 
• The present perfect tense requires the past participle form of the verb, not the base form. The correct form of the verb is "**completed**".
 
• Thus, the correct sentence should be: "**Reh has completed his homework**."
 
• Other options are grammatically correct and appropriately use the present perfect tense with the correct form of the verb: 
 
 
• **Option 1:** "I have completed my task" – correct usage of the present perfect tense.
 
• **Option 2:** "Ram has completed his project" – correct usage of the present perfect tense.
 
• **Option 4:** "Rashi has completed her homework" – correct usage of the present perfect tense.
 
 

Therefore, the correct answer is **Option 3**.

 

**Correct Sentence:** *"Reh has **completed** his homework."*

 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Present Perfect Tense** uses the auxiliary verb "**has/have**" with the **past participle** form of the main verb (e.g., completed, finished, eaten).
 
• The past participle of "complete" is "**completed**," not "complete".

questions.question:
The following sentence has been split into four segments. Identify the segment that contains an error.

I regret / in notify that / the model you want/ is out of stock.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is **Option 4**.

 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The phrase "**in notify**" is grammatically incorrect.
 
• The correct expression should be "**to notify**" as the verb "regret" is followed by an infinitive ("to" + base verb) when expressing formal notification or announcements.
 
• Thus, the corrected sentence should be: "*I regret to notify that the model you want is out of stock.*"
 
• Therefore, the grammatical error lies in **segment 2**.

Therefore, the correct answer is **Option 4**.

 

**Correct Sentence:** *"I regret **to notify** that the model you want is out of stock."*

 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• Use "**regret to + verb**" when expressing formal regret about an action you're doing now or about to do (e.g., regret to inform, regret to announce).
 
• Use "**regret + verb-ing**" when expressing sorrow about a past action (e.g., I regret saying that).

questions.question:
Select the option that will improve the underlined part of the given sentence. In case no improvement is needed, select ‘No improvement required’.

When Shina reached the bus stand, she realised that __she has left her wallet__ at home.

options.text: she had been left her wallet

questions.solution:
The correct answer is **Option 2**.

 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The sentence is written in the **past tense**, as indicated by "reached" and "realised".
 
• The action of **leaving the wallet** occurred **before** Shina realised it, so the **past perfect tense** should be used.
 
• The past perfect form is "**she had left her wallet**", which correctly indicates a completed action before another past action.
 
• Hence, the underlined part "she has left her wallet" must be changed to "**she had left her wallet**".

Therefore, the correct answer is **Option 2**.

 

**Correct Sentence:** *"When Shina reached the bus stand, she realised that **she had left her wallet** at home."*

 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **"Has left"** is present perfect, which is incorrect in a fully past narrative.
 
• **"Leaves"** is simple present; unsuitable for past events.
 
• **"Had been left"** is passive and incorrectly formed here.

questions.question: Select the grammatically correct sentence from the given options.

options.text: He is famous for all his contributions for weekly magazines.
He is famous for all his contributions to weekly magazines.
He is more famous for all his contributions for weekly magazines.
He is more famous for all his contributions to weekly magazines.

questions.solution:
The correct answer is **Option 2**.

 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• In the sentence "**He is famous for all his contributions to weekly magazines**", the preposition "**to**" is used correctly to indicate the direction or target of his contributions.
 
• The correct preposition to use when referring to contributions made to an entity or cause is "**to**" (e.g., contributions to a cause, contributions to a magazine).
 
• Other options are incorrect because they use "**for**" inappropriately: 
 
 
• **Option 1:** "Contributions for weekly magazines" does not convey the intended meaning of contributing to magazines.
 
• **Option 3:** The use of "more famous" is redundant without additional context or comparison. The preposition should still be "to" when talking about contributions.
 
• **Option 4:** "More famous for contributions to" does not make sense grammatically and contextually as it lacks a proper comparison.
 
 

Therefore, the correct answer is **Option 2**.

 

**Correct Sentence:** *"He is famous for all his contributions **to** weekly magazines."*

 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• The preposition "**to**" indicates the direction or target of the action (e.g., contributions to charity, to an organization).
 
• "For" is typically used when indicating the reason for something or in exchange for something (e.g., famous for his skills, paying for a book).

questions.question:
The following sentence has been split into four segments. Identify the segment that contains grammatical error(s).

At the zoo, a curious child / fed an elephant some peanuts, / while enthusiastic group of the visitors / watched in amazement.

options.text: At the zoo, a curious child
while enthusiastic group of the visitors

questions.solution:
The correct answer is **Option 2**.

 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The phrase "**while enthusiastic group of the visitors**" is grammatically incorrect due to a missing article.
 
• Before a singular countable noun like "**group**", an article is required — here, it should be "**an enthusiastic group**".
 
• Also, the phrase "**of the visitors**" is correct, but the article must come before the adjective "enthusiastic" that qualifies "group".
 
• So, the corrected phrase should be: "**while an enthusiastic group of the visitors**".

Therefore, the correct answer is **Option 2**.

 

**Correct Sentence:** *"At the zoo, a curious child fed an elephant some peanuts, while **an enthusiastic group of the visitors** watched in amazement."*

questions.question: From the given options, identify the sentence which is in the positive degree.

options.text: I have a greater idea in this regard.
His brother is an intelligent boy.
She is the most beautiful girl of the class.
They are playing hockey with longer sticks.

questions.solution:

__
 
• The **positive degree** is used to describe a quality without making any comparison, such as simply stating a fact or characteristic.
 
• In the sentence "**His brother is an intelligent boy**," the adjective "intelligent" is in the **positive degree** as it simply describes his brother without comparing him to anyone else.
 
• The other options use comparative or superlative degrees: 
 
 
• **Option 1:** "Greater" is a **comparative degree**, indicating a comparison of two things.
 
• **Option 3:** "Most beautiful" is a **superlative degree**, indicating the highest degree of beauty among a group.
 
• **Option 4:** "Longer" is a **comparative degree**, comparing the sticks to others.
 
 

Therefore, the correct answer is **Option 2**.

 

**Correct Sentence:** *"His brother is an intelligent boy."*

 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• The **positive degree** simply describes a quality without comparing it to others (e.g., smart, beautiful, tall).
 
• The **comparative degree** is used to compare two things (e.g., smarter, more beautiful, taller).
 
• The **superlative degree** is used to compare more than two things and shows the highest or lowest degree of a quality (e.g., smartest, most beautiful, tallest).

From contacting our loved ones to buying groceries for our daily needs, mobile phones fulfilled our every requirement during the COVID-19 pandemic. Not only during the pandemic, but mobile phones have also ________ our needs since the time of their invention.

questions.question: Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank number 1.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is '**gone**'.

 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__** 

__
 
• The sentence is in the **past perfect tense**, which is used to show that an action was completed before another action or time in the past.
 
• The verb **"had"** indicates past perfect, and it must be followed by the **past participle** form of the verb.
 
• The correct past participle of "go" is **"gone"**, making "had gone" the grammatically correct structure.
 
• Other options are incorrect: "went" is simple past, "go" is base form, and "going" is present participle — none of which fit after "had".

Therefore, the correct answer is '**Option 1**'.

 

Complete Sentence: *My parents and younger sister had gone__ to my uncle's house to spend the day.* 

 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **__Additional Information__** 

 
• "Went" (simple past) is used alone for completed past actions (e.g., They went to the market).
 
• "Go" (base form) is used with modals or present forms (e.g., They will go tomorrow).
 
• "Going" (present participle) is used in continuous tenses (e.g., They are going now).

Therefore, the correct answer is '**Option 2**'.

 

Complete Sentence: *My parents and younger sister had gone to my uncle's house to spend__ the day.*

• "Spent" is past tense (e.g., They spent the day at home) — incorrect here.
 
• "Spends" is third person singular present (e.g., She spends too much time reading) — incorrect here.
 
• "Spending" is the gerund or present participle (e.g., Spending time with family is fun) — not used after "to".
